title: Much, Many or A Lot Of?
intro: Much, many or a lot of? It depends on whether you can count the thing. Pick the one that fits.

A2.why: “Money” is uncountable, so questions use “how much”.
“Books” are countable, so questions use “how many”.
Uncountable “time” in a negative: “much”. “A lot” would need “of”.

A2.q: There are ___ students in the class.

A2.why: Uncountable “water” in a positive sentence: “a lot of”.
“Homework” is uncountable, so “a lot of”, not “many”.

A2.q: There isn't ___ sugar in the jar.
I met ___ people at the party.
A2.why: “People” is countable plural; in a positive sentence “a lot of” sounds natural.

A2.q: The cowboys didn't have ___ water in the desert.

B1.q: I have ___ friends here — just two or three.
B1.why: “Just two or three” is a small but positive number: “a few”.

B1.q: She has ___ friends here — she feels lonely.
B1.why: “Lonely” is the clue: “few” means not enough.

B1.q: There's ___ milk left — enough for one coffee.
B1.why: Uncountable and “enough” is the clue: “a little” is positive.

B1.q: There's ___ hope of finding survivors now — it's been ten days.
B1.why: “Ten days” makes it sad news: “little” means almost none.
“Advice” is uncountable, and you want some: “a little”.

B1.q: ___ people showed up — the room was almost empty.
B1.why: “Almost empty” is the clue: “few” means hardly any.

B1.q: We have ___ time before the train leaves — let's hurry.
B1.why: “Let's hurry” is the clue: “little” means not enough.

B1.q: I'd like ___ sugar in my tea, please.
B1.why: Uncountable “sugar”, and you want some: “a little”.

B1.q: ___ of the students passed the exam — most failed.
B1.why: “Most failed” is the clue: “few” means hardly any.

B1.q: Add ___ salt to the soup — just a pinch.
There were ___ doctors in the Wild West, so people often treated themselves.
B1.why: “So people treated themselves” shows there weren't enough: “few”.

B1.q: I've got ___ euros left — enough for a coffee.
B1.why: Countable “euros” and “enough” is the clue: “a few”.

B2.q: There's ___ time — no need to rush.
B2.why: “No need to rush” means more than enough: “plenty of”.

B2.q: A great ___ of research supports this theory.

B2.why: Countable “complaints” takes “a number of”, with a plural verb.

B2.q: The project required a great ___ of patience.
We have ___ of options to choose from.
B2.why: “Plenty of” works with countable and uncountable nouns; the others need “a”.

B2.q: A ___ of the votes went to the new candidate.
B2.why: “A majority of” means more than half.

B2.q: There's a ___ of evidence against him.

B2.why: Countable “people” takes “a number of”; “a great deal” is for uncountables.

B2.q: She spends a great deal ___ time reading.
B2.why: The phrase is always “a great deal of”.

B2.q: There's been a great ___ of rain in Valencia this autumn.
A large ___ of cattle were driven north from Texas.
B2.why: “Cattle” is a plural noun, so “a large number of”.

C1.q: The report offers ___ of information on the topic.
C1.why: “Offers” is positive: “a wealth of” means a large, rich amount.

C1.q: There is ___ of reliable data on this issue.
C1.why: “There is plenty of” has no “a”, so only “a dearth of” (a lack) fits.

C1.q: He earns only ___ of what she does.
C1.why: “Only” is the clue: “a fraction of” means a small part.

C1.q: The team produced ___ notes during the meeting.
C1.why: “Copious notes” is the natural collocation: a lot of them.

C1.q: There's ___ of talented candidates this year.
C1.why: “No shortage of” means plenty; “talented” keeps the tone positive.

C1.q: The museum holds ___ of rare artefacts.
C1.why: A museum “holds” a lot: “an abundance of”.

C1.q: ___ evidence exists to support the claim, so the court accepted it.
C1.why: “The court accepted it” shows there was enough: “ample”.

C1.q: Resources are ___ in this remote region.
C1.why: “Remote” is the clue: “scarce” means hard to find.
An archive “contains” many documents: “a wealth of”.

C1.q: Given the ___ of funding, the project was cancelled.
C1.why: “Cancelled” shows money was missing: “dearth” means a lack.

C1.q: Valencia enjoys ___ of sunshine all year round.
Early surgeons worked with only a ___ of the tools doctors have today.
C1.why: “Only” is the clue: “a fraction of” means a small part.
